claims.text: Introducing a controlled thin surface oxide layer onto metallic transition-metal catalysts improves durability.
A controlled thin surface oxide layer reduces catalyst sintering.
A controlled thin surface oxide layer sustains or enhances catalytic activity and selectivity under reactive, high-temperature conditions.
Mild oxidation under controlled temperature and oxygen partial pressure can form a controlled thin surface oxide layer on the metal particles.
High-temperature redox cycling is a condition under which catalyst sintering typically occurs.
The oxide layer must remain sufficiently thin to avoid blocking active sites.
The pretreatment produces a preformed, adherent thin oxide layer on the metal nanoparticles.
The oxide layer acts as a kinetic barrier that limits metal-atom mobility.
Limiting metal-atom mobility through the oxide layer reduces particle coalescence and sintering.
The oxide–metal interface can preserve adsorption and desorption behavior favorable for catalytic turnover.
Controlled oxidation can alter the electronic environment and adjust intermediate binding energies according to the Sabatier principle.
Oxide-pretreated catalysts will exhibit less particle growth than untreated catalysts under identical high-temperature redox conditions.
Oxide-pretreated catalysts will maintain or improve activity and selectivity relative to untreated catalysts.
Untreated catalysts undergo more pronounced sintering and agglomeration under high-temperature redox conditions.
Sintering of untreated catalysts causes a decline in catalytic performance.
The proposed benefit may fail when the oxide layer becomes excessively thick and passivates the catalyst surface.
The proposed benefit may not apply to catalyst systems that are inherently resistant to sintering.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with catalyst composition, support properties, and reaction conditions.
